lines: Two engineers present the exact same pipeline to the same room.

One shows a single diagram and explains the choice with one word: scalable. The other shows several priced alternatives, names the one actually chosen, and states precisely what would make the team reconsider it.
Much later, demand on that system grows well beyond what either of them originally planned for. Only one of these two engineers finds that growth unsurprising.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
The first engineer already walked in holding a diagram. Simply adding more boxes and more labels to that same diagram wouldn't turn it into something fundamentally different.
So what's actually missing from a plain diagram that a decision genuinely needs?
answer: A diagram, no matter how carefully labeled, is still only a picture of what eventually got built.
It is never, by itself, a record of why that particular thing beat every alternative sitting next to it.
What the second engineer actually walked in holding was a real comparison across options, each with its own cost, plus one specific, named condition under which the whole team would change course.

lines: A genuine decision card holds several distinct alternatives side by side, every one of them priced using the exact same units, and that list always includes simply doing nothing at all.
Whichever alternative actually gets chosen visibly lifts off that same card.
Every other alternative considered stays right there too, clearly visible, because a decision unable to explain why it beat its own alternatives was never really tested in the first place.
Set a single lonely option down right beside that same card holding several real alternatives.
The lonely option can only ever assert that it was chosen. It can never explain why.
Only the card holding real alternatives can actually answer the much harder question of why it specifically won.
Whichever alternative just got chosen now unfolds into its own proper written record.

A short title names it. The surrounding context gets described using plainly neutral language, without quietly favoring any one side of the argument. The decision itself gets written as a clear, active statement.
A status marks where that decision currently stands, and a consequences section lists everything that follows from it, the costs included, never only whatever happened to turn out well.
Two particular fields get added on top of that standard written record.
The actual cost of every alternative that was considered, each one stated using identical units so they can be fairly compared.
And one specific, testable observation. Not some vague sense that circumstances might shift someday, but an actual number that, once it's crossed, means revisiting this exact decision.
A later decision that genuinely reverses an earlier one never simply erases that earlier record.
The old record stays exactly where it was, now clearly marked as superseded, sitting right beside whatever new decision actually replaced it.
That way, anyone reading this later can still see precisely what the team used to believe, and exactly why that belief eventually changed.
Take that exact same pipeline and redraw it with every single arrow running dramatically thicker than before.
Exactly one box in that whole redrawn picture lights up first: the one that genuinely overflows before anything else in the system does.
That specific box is the honest answer to whether this design will actually scale, and it names, quite precisely, what has to be built next.
Several priced alternatives, sitting side by side, are what actually makes a decision real in the first place.
A written record's true value sits in that one added field asking what would ever change the team's mind, far more than in the decision it's actually recording.
A decision that gets reversed stays superseded on the page. It never simply gets edited away as if it had never existed.
And redrawing the same picture with everything running thicker is what finds the very next bottleneck, well before the real load ever does.
One more, to use this for real: a candidate runs through this exact timed exercise, but opens by drawing a detailed diagram before ever stating a single requirement.
Does that early time simply vanish without consequence, or does it eventually show up somewhere later in that same session?
answer: That lost time never simply vanishes, and assuming it does is exactly the wrong read.
A diagram drawn early never actually substitutes for the block of time it quietly skipped past.

Since the whole session runs against one fixed, shared budget, time spent too early always comes directly out of whichever block happens to run last, which is precisely where a candidate ends up feeling that squeeze.
